editorial.headline: Mobile Food Service Meets Bali’s PMA Boundary
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56102 groups temporary food stalls, carts, food trucks and food stands into one activity—nationally open to full foreign ownership, but unavailable to PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through a PT PMA. That local answer is not a judgement on the food concept; it follows the registration structure recorded for the activity. OSS provides no Usaha Besar scale row, leaving the activity reserved for UMKM. Because a PT PMA is treated by law as Usaha Besar, it cannot take this registration route in Bali. The record also notes a permanent, island-wide Bali PMA moratorium for the Low and Medium-Low risk categories it covers; the decisive result for this activity is the structural bar just described.

KBLI 56102 is about providing food to customers from a non-fixed or non-permanent structure. The setting may be capable of moving, dismantling and reassembly, or it may remain in place without those capabilities. What matters is its non-permanent character, rather than a fixed restaurant premises. The scope embraces tented food stalls, travelling food sellers using motorised or non-motorised vehicles, pushcarts, food trucks and food stands. It also includes eating stalls within this temporary-place framework. The code therefore captures food service whose commercial setting is deliberately portable, provisional or otherwise outside a permanent building.

Its listed operating scales are Mikro and Kecil. That is an important part of the activity’s identity: the registration record places this kind of food provision within micro and small enterprise scale, while Bali’s PMA result turns on the absence of an Usaha Besar row. For an operator, the practical reading is straightforward. The business model can be recognisable and familiar—a tent stall, cart, truck or stand—yet the applicable registration route is defined by its scale and structure, not by how polished or ambitious the food concept may be.

Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Put simply, the national record allows this activity to be entirely foreign-owned. Bali does not replace that national ceiling with a different percentage; instead, it closes the PMA registration path through the local scale structure. National openness and Bali registrability are therefore separate questions here. A prospective foreign owner should hold both truths at once: the national ownership position is fully open, while a PT PMA cannot register this activity in Bali under the recorded local conditions.
